title: Input and Output
description: Reading console input with Scanner, and formatting output with System.out and printf.
objectives: Read different types of input using Scanner
Understand System.in and System.out at a conceptual level

content.heading: Reading Input with Scanner
content.body:
java.util.Scanner is the standard way to read console input: Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in); wraps the standard input stream, and methods like nextInt(), nextDouble(), and nextLine() read a value of the corresponding type. A well-known gotcha: nextInt() (and similar numeric methods) only consumes the number itself, leaving the trailing newline character in the input buffer — calling nextLine() immediately afterward then reads that leftover empty line instead of waiting for new input. The fix is an extra throwaway scanner.nextLine() call to consume the leftover newline before reading an actual line of text.

BufferedReader (java.io.BufferedReader, wrapping an InputStreamReader around System.in) is a lower-level, more efficient alternative for reading text, commonly seen in performance-sensitive or competitive-programming contexts, though Scanner is friendlier for typical console I/O.

content.heading: Output with System.out and printf
content.body: System.out.println(x) prints x followed by a newline; System.out.print(x) omits the newline. System.out.printf(format, args...) provides C-style formatted output using format specifiers: %d for integers, %f for floating-point (with optional precision, like %.2f for two decimal places), %s for strings, and %n for a platform-appropriate newline. System.in and System.out are Java's standard input and output streams, conceptually equivalent to stdin/stdout in other languages.

content.explanation: The extra scanner.nextLine() after nextInt() prevents the following nextLine() call from immediately returning an empty string. printf formats the output using %s and %d placeholders.

keyPoints: Scanner(System.in) with nextInt()/nextDouble()/nextLine() reads typed console input
nextInt() leaves a trailing newline that a following nextLine() will immediately consume unless cleared first
System.in/System.out are Java's standard input/output streams
commonMistakes: Calling nextLine() right after nextInt()/nextDouble() and getting an unexpectedly empty string
Forgetting %n (or \n) to add a newline in printf output
Not validating Scanner input, leading to InputMismatchException on unexpected input
